Dress code and safety on the stand

Clay shooting is a public sport, and the rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting ask shooters to dress neatly and practically. The dress code has two purposes: safety and respect for the competition.

The dress rules are almost the same in both disciplines. Shorts must be long: no more than 5 cm above the knee. A top needs sleeves, short ones are enough, and has to come up to the neck, with a collar or a round neck. A vest over a bare chest is not allowed, and sandals are banned for safety.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

At the competition. Sandals are banned there because they are unsafe.

Compak® Sporting

At the station, in practice and in competition: sandals are banned in both.

The competitor number goes on your back, somewhere between the shoulders and the waist. It must be fully visible: not folded and not cut. A breach of the dress or number rules first brings a warning; if it is not put right, the jury can go as far as exclusion.

Tip: Many shooters also wear a cap with a peak against sun and rain, gloves, and carry a cartridge bag for the day's supply. These are custom, not rules.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Hearing protection: for everyone on or near the layout, spectators included; children on the ground must wear it everywhere outside the clubhouse. Glasses: for shooters, referees and staff, and for anyone near a stand.

Compak® Sporting

Hearing protection: for shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the event. Glasses: for shooters, referees and staff.

In both disciplines, a shooter who comes to the stand without hearing protection or safety glasses is treated as absent and cannot shoot. How to choose them: Eye and ear protection.

Safety: Carry the gun open (so that everyone can see it cannot fire), even when it is unloaded. A semi-automatic is carried with the breech open: the bolt is locked back, so you can see the chamber is empty. Its muzzle (the front end of the barrel) points straight up or down. When not in use, the gun stands upright in a gun rack. Nobody touches another shooter's gun without permission. Slings and straps are not allowed in either discipline.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Only on the stand, muzzle down the range, after the referee says shooting may start.

Compak® Sporting

Only on your own station, after the start is allowed. Keep the gun open, muzzle towards the targets and inside the Firing Angle Limiter (the frame around the station that stops the barrels swinging too far). Close it only when it is your turn.

In both disciplines you may put no more than two cartridges into a semi-automatic. After leaving the stand, its user picks up the empty cases the gun has thrown out. Empty cases go in the bin where there is one.

Safety: Before turning around on the stand, open the gun and take out all cartridges, fired or not. During the presentation and any interruption, the gun is open and unloaded. Shoot only in your turn, only at your own target, and not at animals.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Not allowed anywhere at the shooting ground, including swinging along a target's line before you call.

Compak® Sporting

Not allowed off the shooting positions, nor while someone else in your squad is shooting.

Gun and ammunition laws differ from country to country. The FITASC rules apply at the competition, but they do not replace local laws on carrying and storing a shotgun. Before a trip abroad, see Travelling with a gun inside the EU.

Key points

  • Long shorts only (no more than 5 cm above the knee); tops with sleeves (short is fine); no sandals.
  • The competitor number goes on the back, fully visible.
  • Carry the gun open, without a sling; load only on the stand once the referee allows it.
  • Before turning around, open the gun and take out all cartridges.
  • Without hearing protection or glasses, a shooter is treated as absent, in both disciplines.

Did you know?

Each Compak® Sporting station has a frame, the Firing Angle Limiter. It stops the gun from swinging too far and keeps the shooter inside the position.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Ears and eyes on before you walk up.

    Meaning: Put on hearing protection and glasses before approaching the stand.

  • Referee Number on your back, please.

    Meaning: Referee: the competition number must be fully visible on the back.

  • Referee Ears and eyes on.

    Meaning: Put on hearing protection and glasses before the station.

For the interpreter
  • Near the stand you are part of the public: wear protection, keep quiet during the call, and do not comment on a decision. The rules do not mention interpreters, but passing on a coach's advice during a competition can be judged as coaching. Then the shooter gets a yellow card and you are sent out of the shooting area. Interpret only official words for the referee, jury and organiser.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which shorts are allowed at FITASC competitions?

    1. Any sports shorts
    2. No shorts at all
    3. Long ones, near the knee
    Answer

    Long ones, near the knee

    Short shorts are banned; long ones are allowed if they end no more than 5 cm above the knee.

    Chapter 17 · Dress code for competitors

  2. How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold on the stand?

    1. One
    2. Two at most
    3. Three at most
    4. As many as fit
    Answer

    Two at most

    Both rulebooks limit a semi-automatic to no more than two cartridges.

    Chapter 8 · When and how to load

  3. Are gun slings allowed in Compak® Sporting?

    1. No, in neither discipline
    2. Yes, only in Compak® Sporting
    3. Only between stations
    Answer

    No, in neither discipline

    Slings and straps are banned in both disciplines; guns are carried open.

    Chapter 18 · Which guns are allowed
